title: Answers for the teacher
intro: These two worked recommendations illustrate numerical effectiveness and reasoned trade-offs. The first has the highest simulated reduction. The second is a close alternative with a prevention focus. Other valid arrangements may be defensible when supported by evidence.
simulation_note: All counts are invented classroom simulation data for four weeks, from a baseline of 300 pieces.

plans.heading: Option 1 — Highest simulated reduction

allocations.reason: The mall has an outdoor eating area, uncovered bins and discarded food-and-drink packaging. Covered public bins and regular emptying respond to this collection point.
allocations.limitation: Rubbish still needs to be put into the bins, and the emptying service must continue. Bins do not stop disposable packaging being used.

allocations.reason: Rubbish is spread near the entrance and farther across the sand. A cleanup team can collect litter away from the existing entrance bins.
allocations.limitation: New rubbish may appear between weekly visits, so ongoing collection is needed.

allocations.reason: Rain can carry packaging from the kerb into roadside drains. The main drain is accessible to a council maintenance team, making capture and servicing plausible in this scenario.
allocations.limitation: The basket needs emptying and only catches rubbish that reaches the fitted drain.

plans.summary: This arrangement reduces 130 pieces in the four-week simulation, leaving 170. It is the unique highest numerical total under the allocation rule. Much of the approach manages rubbish after disposal rather than reducing disposable consumption.
plans.calculation_policy: Derive displayed effects and totals from actions.json at runtime; expected_total is a validation check, not a second editable effects matrix.

plans.heading: Option 2 — Close alternative with a prevention focus

allocations.reason: Shopkeepers are willing to accept reusable bottles and food containers. Refill/reuse acts on disposable consumption where sellers and customers meet.
allocations.limitation: Customers need to bring and use reusable items; it does not directly collect existing litter.

allocations.reason: The beach is busy with visitors carrying packaged food and drinks. The bin package has its highest simulated effect here, at 50 pieces.
allocations.limitation: Entrance collection points may miss rubbish farther across the sand, and bins still need use and emptying.

allocations.reason: The roadside drain pathway and council access make a serviced litter basket a reasonable fit.
allocations.limitation: It needs maintenance and leaves rubbish outside that drainage route unaddressed.

plans.summary: This arrangement reduces 125 pieces, leaving 175. It gives up five pieces of simulated reduction compared with Option 1 while including prevention of some disposable packaging at the mall. It is second by numerical total, not a second mathematical maximum. The prevention argument is defensible, but the data do not prove better long-term outcomes.
plans.calculation_policy: Derive displayed effects and totals from actions.json at runtime; expected_total is a validation check, not a second editable effects matrix.

comparison_note: A larger total is evidence, not a complete justification. Ask learners to connect the choice to a place clue and recognise a limitation. Distinguish results inside the simulation from judgments about participation, maintenance and future effects.
display_policy: This screen is intentionally reachable in the top navigation without a password, hidden route or warning gate because the website is a university sample. It is not a separate teaching resource or the individual exit slip. Keep the activity screens free of automatic answer selection/scoring.
